title: 3-Read Friday #91
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 91 of Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday curates three posts spanning classroom tools and AI evidence. Barton opens with Anna Sutton's defence of mini-whiteboards, noting that despite being the format's biggest fan he still finds her honest reckoning with their practical challenges and fixes valuable. He then turns to Carl Hendrick's deep dive into emerging evidence on AI tutoring, framing it against Eedi's own new paper with Google DeepMind on supporting human tutors with AI hints. Finally, Barton highlights Larry Cuban's piece on how classroom computer use has become so normalised in American schools that almost nobody still asks whether it improves learning outcomes, adding that he sees the same pattern in the schools he visits. Taken together, the issue pairs a granular classroom-practice post with two pieces interrogating the evidence base behind education technology.
points: Barton frames Sutton's mini-whiteboard piece as a corrective to complacency: even a self-described superfan of MWBs concedes they are underused and worth re-examining for their practical failure points.

AI tutoring is described as 'very much on my mind' for Barton because of Eedi's own new research collaboration with Google DeepMind on AI-assisted human tutoring, which directly informs why he flags Hendrick's evidence review.

Cuban's argument that classroom device use has become so normalised nobody questions it any more is amplified by Barton's own observation that he sees the same pattern of unquestioned tech adoption in the schools he visits.
The issue links a practical classroom-tool post to two evidence-scrutiny pieces, showing Barton's recurring editorial move of pairing craft-level tips with research-literacy prompts.

We recently released our first paper on our collaboration with Google DeepMind, which explores supporting human tutors with AI hints, so AI tutoring is very much on my mind at the moment.
Carl takes a deep dive into the subject, highlighting key considerations for those designing or considering using the technology.

Larry highlights how the use of laptops, tablets and other digital devices in U.S. classrooms has become so normalised that very few teachers, administrators or parents question whether they actually improve learning outcomes.
Meaningful data showing improved academic achievement remains lacking. I see parallels with many of the schools I visit!
